questions.title: Double covalent bonds in carbon dioxide
questions.stimulus: The dot-and-cross diagram shows the arrangement of outer-shell electrons in one molecule of carbon dioxide (CO₂).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the total number of shared pairs of electrons in one CO₂ molecule, and describe the electrostatic attraction in a covalent bond.

points.text: 4 shared pairs of electrons (two double covalent bonds)
Strong electrostatic attraction between the shared pair(s) of electrons and the nuclei of both bonded atoms

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why carbon dioxide has a very low boiling point and is a gas at room temperature.

points.text: Simple molecular substance with weak intermolecular forces between separate CO₂ molecules
Only a small amount of energy is needed to overcome these intermolecular forces

accept: weak forces of attraction between molecules
reject: covalent bonds are broken on boiling

questions.title: Simple molecules and relative molecular mass
questions.stimulus: The diagram shows a dot-and-cross model of ammonia (NH₃), and the table compares the relative molecular mass (Mᵣ) and boiling point of four simple molecular Group 4 hydrides.

parts.label: a
parts.text: From the diagram of NH₃, state the number of shared pairs and the number of unshared (lone) pairs of electrons on the nitrogen atom.

reject: 6 shared pairs (counting electrons instead of pairs)

parts.label: b
parts.stimulus: The table compares the relative molecular mass (Mᵣ) and boiling point of four simple molecular Group 4 hydrides.
parts.text: Use the table to explain why the boiling point increases from CH₄ to SnH₄.

points.text: Relative molecular mass (Mᵣ) / molecule size increases from CH₄ to SnH₄
The intermolecular forces between the molecules become stronger
More (thermal) energy is needed to overcome the intermolecular forces

reject: more covalent bonds to break on boiling

questions.title: Structures and properties of carbon allotropes
questions.stimulus: The diagram shows schematic models of three forms (allotropes) of pure carbon, labelled A, B and C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Structure C is a giant covalent structure. Explain why structure C is a solid with a very high melting point.

points.text: Contains many strong covalent bonds between carbon atoms throughout a giant covalent lattice
A large amount of (thermal) energy is needed to break these strong covalent bonds

accept: diamond — each carbon forms 4 strong covalent bonds

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why structure B (graphite) conducts electricity and is soft enough to act as a lubricant.

points.text: Conducts electricity: each carbon forms only 3 covalent bonds, leaving delocalised electrons free to move along the layers and carry charge
Soft / lubricant: only weak forces between layers, so the layers can slide over each other easily

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why structure A (C₆₀ fullerene) has a much lower melting point than structure C.

points.text: C₆₀ fullerene is a simple molecular substance made of separate C₆₀ spheres with weak intermolecular forces between molecules
Much less energy is needed to overcome these weak intermolecular forces than to break the many strong covalent bonds in diamond
